Who Transfers Safety? Identifying and Targeting Cross-Lingual Shared Safety Neurons

Identify shared safety neurons that connect high-resource and non-high-resource language behaviour.

Zhang Xianhui · Xie Chengyu · Zhu Linxia · Yang Yonghui · Zhao Weixiang · Cheng Zifeng · Wang Cong · Shen Fei · Chua Tat-Seng

February 1, 2026 ·ICML 2026 ·Read the paper ·PDF ·Code
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

This study identifies a small set of safety neurons shared across languages and tests their role through masking and targeted training. Their overlap connects safety behavior in high-resource and non-high-resource languages. SS-Neuron Expansion focuses optimization on the English safety neurons used as a bridge for cross-lingual transfer.

The evidence combines neuron-level interventions with multilingual attack evaluations. This connects an observed language disparity to a candidate internal mechanism, then asks whether training that mechanism improves safety across languages.

SharedCross-lingual safety neurons
CausalActivation and suppression tests
TargetedSelected-neuron alignment

Cross-language safety transfer depends on which internal mechanisms languages share and can actually access.

Why this matters

A model’s safety behaviour can differ sharply across languages. Understanding which internal components participate in that transfer can guide more focused alignment.

How it works

  1. Identify monolingual safety neurons and test their role through activation and suppression.
  2. Find the subset shared between high-resource and non-high-resource languages.
  3. Train the selected shared subset with a strategy accounting for language resources and model architecture.

What the study finds

Suppressing shared neurons causes concurrent safety drops in non-high-resource languages, while reinforcement improves cross-lingual consistency. Targeted fine-tuning reports stronger non-high-resource safety than the compared methods while maintaining general capabilities.

What this means

A multilingual model can share parameters without sharing equally effective access to a safety mechanism. Locating the bridge helps make that distinction concrete and offers a principled target for allocating alignment effort where language coverage is uneven.

The broader research direction is mechanism-aware transfer: first identify what is shared, then test whether strengthening it benefits languages beyond those directly supervised. The quality of that transfer must be assessed together with general usefulness and language-specific failure modes.
